clinicalPearls: Most commonly affects the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and palate, causing nasal obstruction, epistaxis, facial swelling, and destructive midfacial ulceration
More prevalent in East Asian and Central/South American populations and strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus in essentially all cases
Extranasal disease can involve skin, testis, gastrointestinal tract, and soft tissue and generally carries a worse prognosis

Tumour cells are usually of NK-cell (or less often cytotoxic T-cell) origin, expressing CD56, cytoplasmic CD3-epsilon, and cytotoxic molecules, with EBV-encoded RNA positivity by in situ hybridisation
The classic histology is angiocentric and angiodestructive growth with prominent necrosis, which can render small biopsies non-diagnostic
Circulating EBV DNA can serve as a marker of disease burden and treatment response
Management commonly combines radiotherapy for localised nasal disease with non-anthracycline, asparaginase-containing chemotherapy regimens
reference.pathophysiology: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is an Epstein-Barr virus-driven neoplasm arising most often from natural killer cells and occasionally cytotoxic T-cells. Latent EBV infection contributes to malignant transformation, and the tumour cells characteristically invade and destroy blood vessel walls (angiocentric and angiodestructive growth), producing ischaemic necrosis and the destructive midfacial lesions historically termed lethal midline granuloma. Overexpression of P-glycoprotein and other drug-efflux mechanisms underlies resistance to anthracycline-based chemotherapy, which is why asparaginase-containing regimens and radiotherapy are preferred. Extensive necrosis can make representative sampling difficult.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other destructive midfacial vasculitides
Invasive fungal sinusitis such as mucormycosis or aspergillosis
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the sinonasal region
Squamous cell carcinoma or other sinonasal malignancy
Chronic invasive bacterial infection or cocaine-induced midline destruction
Other peripheral T-cell lymphomas involving extranodal sites
additionalInvestigations: Deep, representative biopsy avoiding necrotic areas, with immunohistochemistry (CD56, CD3-epsilon, cytotoxic markers)
In situ hybridisation for EBV-encoded RNA
Plasma or whole-blood EBV DNA quantification
MRI of the sinonasal region and skull base to define local extent
PET-CT for staging and detection of extranasal disease
Bone marrow examination and assessment for haemophagocytic syndrome
redFlags: Extensive midfacial or orbital destruction threatening vision or the skull base
Systemic or disseminated (extranasal) disease with rapid progression
Airway compromise from nasopharyngeal or palatal involvement
reference.prognosis: Localised nasal disease treated with combined radiotherapy and asparaginase-based chemotherapy can achieve durable remission, whereas advanced, extranasal, or relapsed disease and secondary haemophagocytosis carry a poor prognosis.
pitfalls: Non-diagnostic biopsies because of extensive necrosis, leading to delayed diagnosis
Mistaking destructive nasal disease for vasculitis or invasive fungal infection
Using anthracycline-based regimens that are relatively ineffective owing to drug efflux
Failing to monitor EBV DNA as a marker of response and relapse
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
management: Anchor management at an experienced lymphoma center given the rarity of this disease

For localized low-risk disease (younger age, stage I, no primary tumor invasion, normal LDH, good performance status), radiation therapy alone to the involved nasal or upper aerodigestive field is an accepted primary approach
For localized disease with risk factors, combined-modality treatment sequencing early radiation therapy with systemic chemotherapy is preferred over chemotherapy first or radiotherapy alone
Concurrent chemoradiation with a platinum-based radiosensitizer followed by non-anthracycline combination chemotherapy is a reasonable option for higher-risk localized disease at expert centers
Anthracycline-containing regimens (such as CHOP-type chemotherapy) have not shown survival benefit and should not be relied upon in this disease, for either localized or disseminated presentations
Non-anthracycline regimens, favoring asparaginase-containing or platinum/etoposide-based combinations, are the preferred systemic backbone

For disseminated (stage III to IV) or extranasal disease, asparaginase-containing multi-agent regimens have shown meaningful response rates and survival and are preferred over anthracycline-based therapy
Consider intermediate-dose methotrexate as part of the regimen where CNS risk factors are present, given its association with decreased CNS relapse

Consider consolidative autologous or allogeneic stem cell transplantation in eligible responders with high-risk or relapsed/refractory disease, individualized with a transplant-capable lymphoma service
For relapsed or refractory disease, asparaginase-containing regimens remain a reasonable option where not already used
Actively consider clinical trial referral for relapsed/refractory or disseminated disease given the rarity of the disease and limited evidence base
Surgery has no established curative role and is limited to diagnostic biopsy and management of local complications, not disease-directed resection
Monitor EBV viral load alongside imaging for surveillance, since viral load at diagnosis and after therapy predicts progression-free and overall survival
Evaluate patients with multiple prognostic risk factors (B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH, lymph node involvement) for CNS involvement and consider CNS-directed staging or prophylaxis
